title: Yesterday far, today close (7:6)
hookLine: great is return: yesterday distant, today near
tomorrow: someone changed. can you still bring up what they did?

lines: SILENT FOR A YEAR: HI EVERYONE.
PEACE TO THE FAR AND THE NEAR.
cards: A family group chat. Someone who's been silent for a year finally types: hi everyone. Who gets the first reply, the cousin who vanished or the aunt who never missed a birthday?
Isaiah has a verse with that question folded inside it. God says: peace, peace, to the one who is far off and to the one who is near. Far comes first.
In the Talmud, two sages read that order, and they disagree about who the far one even is.

teach.b: Rabbi Abbahu says the far one is the person who was far and came back. They're greeted first, and that's why, he says, returners stand where the completely righteous can't. Rabbi Yohanan reads it the other way.

Far off means far from wrongdoing from the start: the one who never went near it. Near means someone who was close to wrongdoing and has only now pulled away. On his reading, the steady one is greeted first.
Let both make their case. Abbahu: the verse puts far first, and coming back from far takes more.
Yohanan: a life that never strayed is no small thing; that steadiness is its own hard-won work.
Maimonides, in his law book, quotes Abbahu's side. And then, in chapter seven, he paints the change at its sharpest. Return, he writes, brings near those who were far.
Yesterday this person was distant, even hateful before God; today, beloved, close, a friend.
A few lines on: yesterday they cried out and weren't answered; today they're answered at once. One day apart. Notice what neither sage says.
Neither says the returner is unwelcome. They argue about who's greeted first, not about the door. Both readings keep the peace, peace for both.

how: Isaiah 57:19, 'peace, peace, to the far and to the near,' is read on Yom Kippur morning in the prophetic reading, and Berakhot 34b's debate over it is a classic text in Jewish study of return.

o: nearness to God depends on a spotless past
the distant are forgiven, but only after a long wait
return closes the distance between a person and God

games.q: who reads it how — tap the pairs.
p: far means the one who came back
far means the one who never strayed
peace to the far and to the near

s: the Talmud agrees that returners outrank the righteous
Abbahu says so; Yohanan reads the same verse the other way. Maimonides quotes Abbahu.
in Isaiah's verse, the far one is greeted first
peace, peace, to the far and to the near. the argument is over who 'far' is.
Rabbi Yohanan thinks returners should be turned away
he argues about who's greeted first, not about the door.

games.q: your class debate puts you on Rabbi Yohanan's side. what's his strongest case?
o: a life that never strayed has its own hard-won steadiness.
people who slip shouldn't be let back in at all.
Isaiah puts the far one second, so Abbahu misread it.
games.why: Yohanan never shuts the door. he reads 'far' as far from wrongdoing and honors a steady life. Maimonides quotes Abbahu, but both views stay on the page.

practice: Pick up your phone and find one person you've drifted from: no fight, just distance. Write them one short, true line, something like: thought of you today. Send it or save it; either way, notice how short the distance was to cross.
Then put the phone face down and rest.

wordCard.voice: Yesterday far: Maimonides' picture of return. One day apart, and the distant one is beloved, close, a friend.

orig.note: Hebrew: to the far and to the near. Isaiah 57:19, the words the sages argue over.

carryVoice: Keep this one: yesterday far, today close, and the sages argued about the order, never the door. Day twenty of the laws, done.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b (Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan on 'far' and 'near')
Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 7:4, 7:6–7 (return brings near the distant; yesterday hated and distant, today beloved, near, a friend; yesterday unanswered, today answered at once)
